# IELTS Academic Writing Task 1 — pie-chart lesson

**Source:** IELTS Advantage, [IELTS Writing Task 1: Ace Pie Charts in Minutes](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=tgwibVefUKk), 23 m 28 s.  
**Transcript:** complete auto-generated English captions exported and reviewed (277 lines). The lesson walks through two pie charts comparing Swiss watch-market shares in 2020 and 2021.

## 1. Understand the task before the values

- Read the task statement to identify the subject, categories, units, and time period.
- Treat the instruction to “select and report the main features” as a selection task. Do not report every slice merely because it is visible.
- Ask what the charts are designed to compare. In the demonstration, they compare six brands and their shares across two years.
- Do not worry if the topic or brand names are unfamiliar; the task is to interpret the visual and report its information, not to show topic expertise.

The video reframes the pie charts as a way to make raw data easier to compare. It then uses the same four-part “pyramid” as the [Academic Task 1 beginner course](writing-task1-academic-beginners-2026.md): paraphrased introduction, broad overview, and two logically grouped detail paragraphs.

## 2. Find the overview — 8:26–13:42

The instructor proposes two main questions:

1. What is the single most striking feature of the data?
2. What was the purpose of showing these categories and time periods?

For the sample, Rolex is the largest brand in both years and increases its share, while all other brands decline. A newspaper headline or a short report to a manager can help the learner state the main result simply. The “stranger test” asks whether someone could understand the main point from the overview without reading the detailed paragraphs.

The video advises choosing two to four broad features and omitting detailed percentages from the overview. Treat that as a practice scaffold. The official criterion is that the response presents a clear overview of key features; it does not prescribe a fixed number of features or prohibit every overview figure. Avoid turning the overview into a second data list.

## 3. Choose logical detail groups — 13:43–17:16

Before writing, compare possible groupings:

- one year per paragraph;
- largest brands versus smaller brands;
- brands that rose versus those that fell.

The instructor rejects a year-by-year split for this example because it makes cross-year comparisons awkward. A “rose versus fell” split gives only one brand in one group. He therefore groups the three largest brands in one paragraph and the remaining three in the other. The useful lesson is to choose groups that make comparison clear and give each paragraph enough information to develop; a fixed grouping will not suit every chart.

Begin a detail paragraph by signaling its group (for example, the three largest brands). This helps the reader see the organization. Compare the same categories across time, include the most informative values, and describe a change in rank when it is more meaningful than a small percentage movement.

## 4. Report important values accurately — 17:16–23:16

The sample uses several useful techniques:

- Use “respectively” after a list of categories and numbers when the order makes the pairing clear.
- Use a proportion such as “almost half” for 46.7% when a rounded description is accurate; exact percentages can also be used when they matter.
- Approximate grouped values only when the approximation is accurate. The small brands are described as being around one tenth each and declining by about one percentage point.
- Report a significant rank change: Cartier overtakes Omega for second place, while Audemars Piguet moves from the smallest share to fourth place.
- Omit a category when it does not add a key feature, but make sure the overall comparison remains adequate.

The source’s rule is to report only the main features, not every slice. Keep an audit trail during practice: circle each value used in the response and verify it against the chart.

## 5. Practice and review

1. Read the prompt and labels; name the categories, measure, and comparison.
2. Write a one-sentence statement of the chart’s purpose.
3. Identify the major overall pattern and two or three additional features worth reporting.
4. Choose a logical grouping for the two detail paragraphs.
5. Draft the introduction and overview, then add selected values and comparisons.
6. Check that the response is accurate, organized, relevant, and long enough; review language and spelling.

The lesson’s “two to four features,” four-paragraph structure, and no-conclusion preference are instructor scaffolds. IELTS Academic Task 1 requires at least 150 words and assesses task achievement, coherence and cohesion, lexical resource, and grammatical range and accuracy. The 150–200 target appears in other source videos but is not a formal maximum. ([IELTS Academic Writing format](https://ielts.org/take-a-test/test-types/ielts-academic-test/ielts-academic-format-writing); [IELTS Writing key assessment criteria](https://ielts.org/cdn/ielts-guides/ielts-writing-key-assessment-criteria.pdf))

## Source-specific caveats

- The instructor says an effective overview is required to score above Band 6. The official descriptors assess overview and key-feature coverage; do not teach the video’s simplified band cutoff as a precise scoring formula.
- Omitting minor slices can improve focus, but the selected details still need to represent the task adequately.
- “No data in the overview” is a useful classroom distinction between overview and details, not a universal official prohibition.
- The sample is a teaching demonstration, not an independent score report.
